Area.evidence_source: The predominant epidemiological pattern of suicide is one of mortality rates three to four times higher among men4 , which is usually explained by biologicist arguments that include greater lethality of means used by men5 .Authors have been pointing out9,22,23 that economic crises lead to men's failure as family providers; this produces conflict, consumption of alcohol and other drugs, emotional suffering and as a last resort suicide. Men have greater suicide mortality rates in societies where hegemonic male roles are in crisis; in such societies men find it difficult to fulfill their normative work-related role24 and they see their identity at risk.Male elderly individuals, on the other hand, are at risk when they step away from work, when there are relationship conflicts or in situations where their codes of honor and masculinity are threatened.Work, as an activity that promotes social integration and autonomy, may be a protection factor for both genders; higher suicide rates have been observed in unemployed individuals21.
